title: Thinking About Filing for Child Custody in Colorado?

content.rendered:
If you’re thinking about filing for child custody in Colorado, it’s important to understand how the process works before taking the first step. Many parents are surprised to learn that Colorado doesn’t actually use the term “child custody.” Instead, the law refers to parental responsibilities, which include parenting time and decision-making responsibilities.

Understanding these concepts and what the court considers when making decisions can help you prepare for the process and focus on what matters most—your child’s well-being.

Colorado Doesn’t Use the Term “Child Custody”

Although many people refer to child custody, Colorado law uses the term parental responsibilities.

Parental responsibilities include two important components:

  • Parenting Time: The schedule that determines when the child spends time with each parent.
  • Decision-Making Responsibility: Which parent (or both parents) has the authority to make important decisions regarding the child’s education, healthcare, religion, and other major issues.

Understanding this terminology can make it easier to navigate the legal process and communicate effectively with your attorney.

The Court Focuses on the Child’s Best Interests

When deciding parenting arrangements, Colorado courts focus on one primary factor: the best interests of the child.

Rather than focusing on what either parent wants, the court evaluates what arrangement will provide the healthiest and most stable environment for the child.

Some of the factors the court may consider include:

  • The child’s emotional and physical well-being.
  • Stability in the child’s daily life.
  • Each parent’s ability to provide a safe and supportive home.
  • The willingness of each parent to encourage a healthy relationship with the other parent.

Why Stability, Safety, and Communication Matter

Courts generally favor arrangements that promote consistency for children.

Maintaining routines, ensuring a safe environment, and demonstrating respectful communication with the other parent can all have a positive impact during a parenting case.

Parents who show they are committed to working together for the benefit of their child often place themselves in a stronger position throughout the legal process.

Demonstrating Your Involvement as a Parent

One way parents can demonstrate their involvement is by showing they actively participate in their child’s life.

Examples include:

  • Attending parent-teacher conferences.
  • Taking the child to medical or dental appointments.
  • Participating in school events and extracurricular activities.
  • Being involved in the child’s daily routine.

These examples can help demonstrate an ongoing commitment to the child’s care and well-being.

Is Parenting Time Always 50/50?

Many parents wonder whether parenting time is automatically divided equally.

In Colorado, 50/50 parenting time is common, but it is not guaranteed.

Every family is different, and the court considers each family’s unique circumstances before determining the parenting schedule.

Factors such as the family’s history, each parent’s involvement, the child’s needs, and other relevant circumstances may influence the final arrangement.

Focus on Cooperation Whenever Possible

Regardless of the circumstances, maintaining a respectful and cooperative relationship with the other parent can benefit both your child and your case.

While disagreements may arise, demonstrating a willingness to communicate and prioritize your child’s needs is often viewed favorably throughout the legal process.

We’re Here to Help

If you’re planning to file for parental responsibilities in Colorado, understanding your rights and responsibilities is an important first step.
